source.title: Emergent Misalignment Can Be Induced by Sycophancy and Reversed via Alignment Gating
source.authors: Sicheng Wang; Xiang-Yang Zhu; Han Wang; Zong-Rui Wang; Yuan Tian; Kai-Wei Zhang; Kai-Yuan Ji; Qi Jia; Guang-Tao Zhai

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether fine-tuning on misaligned examples affects harmful-request acceptance, but the reported acceptance results use a learned gating module rather than ordinary LoRA fine-tuning.
record.gate_note: The paper reports broad emergent-misalignment rates after ordinary LoRA fine-tuning, but those are scores on open-ended prompts, not harmful-request compliance or refusal rates, so they are not rows for these claim versions. Its directly relevant harmful-request acceptance results are in Table 3, where only the gating modules are trained. Benign-data re-fine-tuning results concern the open-ended EM measure, not harmful-request acceptance. The paper does not measure per-token KL, compliant-prefill or suffix bypasses, decoding changes, or safety localization in a small set of parameters.
record.test_reason: Fine-tuning Qwen3 models on narrow misaligned or sycophantic advice data sharply raises StrongREJECT harmful-request acceptance over the base models. This bears on V1 in a new setting: sycophancy or EM data, gate-only training, and 6,000 examples per domain.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. Add that the authors report inverted gates cut StrongREJECT acceptance to near or below base, with about a 1% MMLU cost, and that gates generalize across domains, including onto LoRA-misaligned models.
record.recipe_differences: The relevant harmful-request results use gating modules trained on misaligned data, with the rest of the model frozen; they do not use the original ordinary fine-tuning recipe or its few-to-hundreds-example scale.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported acceptance rates vary across model size and training-data domain.

fits_no_version.finding: Inverting the learned all-layer attention gates (g_inv = 2 − g) without training drops StrongREJECT acceptance to 0.3–6.1%, sometimes below base (Table 4). Inverted gates attached to misaligned LoRA models give 3.8–8.2% (Tables 5, 17-19).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gate-inversion training-free reversal of fine-tuning-induced harmful compliance

fits_no_version.finding: 150 steps of benign re-SFT on a misaligned LoRA model cut StrongREJECT acceptance from 99.4% to 4.0% (Table 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign re-fine-tuning restores refusal after harmful fine-tuning

record.problems: The directly relevant acceptance measurements are from only two model sizes and use gating-module training rather than ordinary model fine-tuning. Results are reported without uncertainty estimates. The sample-size claim in V1 is not tested: the paper uses 6,000 examples per domain.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1 and 2 report open-ended emergent-misalignment rates after LoRA fine-tuning, not harmful-request acceptance or refusal, so those results are excluded. Table 4 reports harmful-request acceptance after gate inversion, but that mitigation condition does not test the versions here.

untested.parts: Few-to-few-hundred example scale: every run uses 6,000 examples per domain. No fine-tuning on explicit harmful-request/compliance pairs: the data is incorrect or unsafe advice and sycophantic agreement.
Not tested. Benign re-SFT is applied only to an already misaligned model, as mitigation.
Not tested as safety localization. The gates cover every attention layer, and the Jaccard overlap analysis concerns suppression positions, not safety weights.

missing.what: StrongREJECT acceptance after ordinary LoRA fine-tuning on sycophancy data, Qwen3-8B: medicine 99.4%, security 98.6%, law 97.9% (base 3.8%). This is the closest-to-original recipe in the paper.

record.verdict_notes: Table 3 text is column-scrambled. The 14B traditional values in the record were shifted, which is fixed above using the overall-average check. Neither original source is this paper, so verdicts are allowed. The LoRA rows are missing from the record because rows_left_out only excluded Tables 1, 2 and 4.

versions.untested_parts: The tested training uses 6,000 examples per domain, not a few to a few hundred; the reported acceptance results come from gating-module training, not ordinary fine-tuning of the model weights.
The paper does not test whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning raises harmful-request acceptance.
No per-token KL divergence or response-position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change bypass test.
The paper trains gates in every attention layer; it does not test whether a small set of model weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
The paper does not test why safety behaviour might be shallow.
The paper does not train or evaluate safety behaviour spread across response tokens.

relation.reason: Own experiments measure harmful-request acceptance after narrow-domain training against unmodified model baselines.

tranche.reason: Tests safety degradation in a new narrow-domain sycophancy/EM setting, chiefly through gate-only training on frozen Qwen3 models with 6,000 examples per domain.

source_check.notes: Section 4.2 specifies 6,000 examples per domain and two epochs with only added gates trained; these results do not establish V1's small-dose clause. StrongREJECT acceptance uses a binary external judge over 313 requests, rather than the benchmark's graded score.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Medicine and security sycophancy data with the gating-module training setup
reader_labels.reason: Acceptance rose from the base rates to 91.7% and 95.5% for medicine and 93.9% for security (R1, R13, R15).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Other tested domains and overall results
reader_labels.reason: Acceptance increased substantially but was below near-total compliance in these settings; results also varied by domain and model (R2–R12, R14, R16–R24). The training used 6,000 examples per domain and trained gates rather than ordinary model fine-tuning.
